blocks.text:
## Can interpretable machine learning predict divorce better?

**We trained the models and tested them on people excluded from fitting.** On the full co-resident couple panel—5,735 respondents, 726 divorces and 82,039 person-years—the enriched additive model had the best held-out point score: **3.40% less prediction loss than a constant-rate model**. Splines plus pair interactions achieved 2.89%; shallow trees achieved about 2.3%–2.4%. More complexity did not improve on the enriched additive model in this comparison. These percentages are loss reductions, **not accuracy, percentage points of divorce risk or causal effects**.

For individuals who were currently married at baseline, the additive model improved loss by about 1.94%, compared with 0.67%/0.37% for depth 2/3 trees. Including already-separated people increased apparent predictive gains to about 13%, because separation identifies marriages already on a dissolution path. That is useful for describing an existing marriage’s status, but does not make a prospective spouse-selection rule.

The models can describe broad risk variation, but this is not a validated personal divorce calculator. Most people do not divorce during an observed interval; always predicting “no divorce” would appear accurate while providing little useful information. We use held-out event-rate loss and calibration rather than that misleading accuracy statistic.

blocks.title: Held-out prediction loss: compare within each population

blocks.text:
### What went into the models—and what did not

The couple model uses both spouses’ schooling, combined wages, earnings split, current age and marriage duration/order, survey wave and respondent sex. The enriched version adds the respondent’s baseline credential, work-hour group, age at first marriage, family income and **own prior religious attendance**. Zero wages and unknown wages are distinct; the full panel retains both-zero and missing-earnings configurations. Income cutpoints, imputers, encoders and splines are learned within training folds.

The individual model uses own education, income position, work hours, age, age at first marriage, sex, wave and prior attendance, with a separate analysis including/excluding already-separated respondents. Neither model includes measured relationship quality, fidelity, wealth or business valuation. The couple model lacks full spouse religious histories and harmonized occupations. Attendance is not denomination or agreement between spouses. The original profile model did not adjust for religion; the enriched prediction model does.

ACS and NSFG are not stacked onto these NLSY observations: ACS current occupation/income can follow the divorce, and NSFG historical dissolution has a different outcome and exposure. “All data” requires harmonized measurement and compatible targets, not merging unrelated survey respondents or treating post-divorce variables as predictors.

### A readable tree is an explanation of a fitted model, not a discovered law

The fitted two-level couple tree groups marriages at about 11 and 18.4 years, then splits older-duration marriages at age 52.5. Its four fitted training leaves have rates around 16.4, 9.6, 6.9 and 2.7 divorces per 1,000 person-years. These thresholds were chosen by an algorithm to summarize this training sample. **They do not overturn the earlier finding that no specific anniversary cutoff was established**, and this tree did not outperform the enriched additive model on held-out people.

The legally-married individual tree first asks whether the respondent was already separated. Its main apparent performance advantage comes from distinguishing that state. Readable tree paths, leaf support, coefficients, calibration tables and trained model files are included in the reproducibility package.

Aggregate calibration is also not enough for portability: the enriched couple model’s observed/expected ratio was about 0.996 in respondent cross-validation, but about 0.870 in a later-wave check—overprediction when applied forward in calendar time. The later-wave test can include people seen earlier, so it is a temporal sensitivity rather than an independent external validation.

## How large are the earnings associations in everyday terms?

The original adjusted model gives balanced-earner incidence of 8.69 divorces per 1,000 married person-years, compared with 6.31 for husband-majority dual earnings, 8.11 for husband-only wages and 12.44 for wife-majority dual earnings. Thus:

- Husband-majority dual versus balanced: **2.38 fewer per 1,000 years**, about 0.238 percentage points per year; RR 0.73.
- Husband-only versus balanced: **0.58 fewer per 1,000 years**, about 0.058 points; its interval includes no difference.
- Wife-majority dual versus balanced: **3.75 more per 1,000 years**, about 0.375 points; the absolute-difference interval is approximately−0.02 to 7.52 per 1, 000. The relative interval is 1.03–1.99; scale-dependent interval approximations give different boundary results, so a large adverse causal effect is not established.

**Husband-only versus husband-majority dual earning must be tested directly.** The direct difference is **+1.81 per 1,000 person-years (95% CI -0.26 to 3.87)**, RR **1.29 (0.98–1.69)**. The point estimate favors both earning, but the original full-sample interval includes no difference. You cannot prove the two configurations differ just because only one comparison against balanced earnings is significant.

Both 16+schooling versus both 12 years corresponds to about 3.41 fewer divorces per 1,000 person-years—0.341 percentage points—conditional on the specified model. It is a broad schooling contrast, not proof that each extra graduate degree improves outcomes. These annual rates cannot be multiplied into fixed-duration or lifetime probabilities.

### What is adjusted, and how much does religion change it?

The original contrasts adjust for both partners’ schooling, combined wages, age, marriage duration, first/subsequent marriage, survey wave and respondent sex. **They do not adjust for religion, occupation, wealth, children or relationship quality.**

In a separate attendance-complete subset, refitting the original profile specification gives husband-only versus husband-majority dual RR 1.320; adding own prior attendance gives RR 1.320. Their approximate intervals are 1.002–1.740 and 1.002–1.738. The small shift indicates that this measured attendance variable explains little of that fitted contrast. The subset itself differs from the original full sample, whose RR was 1.286 with an interval including 1. This is a fragile, nominally bounded result—not a robust recommendation to change spouses’ work arrangements. It also does not establish adjustment for both partners’ beliefs or religious agreement.

## Bachelor’s, master’s, professional and PhD—by occupation

A new original ACS cross-tab supplies all four credentials by sex and predefined broad occupations, with all 80 replicate-weight confidence intervals. It includes 425,403 people and 4,556 past-year divorce reports;41 of 80 cells meet the descriptive support screen. Use the search field to find a credential, sex or occupation. The full table is provided rather than selecting whichever profession has the smallest estimate.

**This table is a different supporting outcome:** crude past-year divorce-report percentages, measured alongside current or recent occupation. A divorce may have preceded a job change. It is not a prospective annual marriage hazard and is not fed into the prediction models. The currently-employed-only sensitivity is supplied separately.

A professional-degree category does not distinguish MD from JD; a doctorate category does not identify a specific PhD field. Occupation is not the same as degree subject. Graduate-degree and profession pairings for both spouses remain limited by available pre-divorce histories and cell sizes. The earlier 16+schooling result does not imply that master’s, professional and doctoral couples form a uniformly safer hierarchy.

blocks.text:
## Couple pairings associated with lower annual divorce incidence

The primary goal is to identify supported lower-rate **couple profiles**, then compare the size of the measured associations. This new joint analysis uses **5,295 respondents, 592 observed divorces and 69,185 person-years**, with both partners' schooling and earnings measured before follow-up. Every adjusted profile uses the same weighted age, marriage-duration, first-versus-subsequent-marriage, calendar-wave and respondent-sex target.

Among the supported combinations tested, **both spouses with 16+ years of schooling, upper-quartile combined wages and both earning with the husband contributing more than 60%** had the lowest model estimate: **4.56 divorces per 1,000 married person-years (approximate 95% CI 3.40–6.11)**. The corresponding balanced-earner profile was **6.29 (4.66–8.48)**. These are exploratory, model-dependent profiles in an older U.S. cohort, not a statistically proven global optimum.

The data do **not** establish that zero wages for the wife improves this profile. Its matching high-schooling/high-combined-wage cell contains only four observed divorces, so its adjusted profile estimate is withheld. The broader husband-only versus balanced comparison below is uncertain. The earlier crude high-husband-wage comparison likewise did not establish an advantage over two high earners.

blocks.text:
### What qualifies as a supported profile?

These nine illustrative archetypes were chosen for the stated questions rather than by searching every possible trait combination for a minimum. Estimates are displayed only with at least **100 distinct respondents and 10 observed divorces** in the matching cell. This exploratory support rule does not guarantee reliable prediction; estimates with 11–19 events remain fragile and borrow strength from the pooled model. Low-event cells remain visible without a modeled ranking.

“Both 12” means 12 completed school years each; “both 16+” pools 16–17 and 18+ years with one fixed observed partner-tier mixture. These are **schooling tiers, not verified bachelor's/master's/PhD credentials**. Q1 and Q4 are within-wave quartiles of **positive combined wage/salary earnings**, not fixed salaries, total household resources or wealth. Both-zero wage couples are outside this model. An annual rate is not a lifetime probability, and multiplying it by marriage length does not produce a valid long-run forecast.

## Which measured differences have the biggest association?

The following comparisons all use **additional or fewer divorces per 1,000 married person-years**, with the other modeled characteristics held to a common distribution. This makes their scale comparable; the chosen changes still differ in size and meaning.

The two-spouse schooling contrast and the husband-majority/both-working contrast show lower annual incidence in this model. The wife-majority point estimate is higher, but its **absolute-difference interval includes zero**; the log-rate-ratio interval differs slightly because the uncertainty transformations use different scales. We lead with absolute differences rather than selecting the more favorable significance result.

**Upper-quartile combined wages alone do not show a clear independent advantage over the lowest quartile once both schooling levels and earnings split are controlled.** This is narrower than the earlier unadjusted high-earner pattern and does not show that raising earnings has no benefit. Husband-only versus balanced is also unresolved. This ranks only the specified contrasts, not every possible cause of divorce.

blocks.title: Standardized associations: first group minus reference

blocks.text:
### How to use this profile

The supported descriptive sketch is **two partners with substantial schooling and adequate combined earnings**, with a husband-majority dual-earner configuration worth further replication. The data do not justify requiring a nonworking wife, a particular religion, party or ethnicity as part of an ideal profile. Separate religion, politics and demographic analyses below have different coverage and should not be multiplied into this joint prediction.

These profiles describe marriages already intact and co-resident at baseline, largely in midlife; they do not forecast the outcomes of people choosing partners today. Schooling and income selection, earlier relationship problems, children, health, age gaps, wealth and unmeasured relationship quality can explain differences. Both-zero wages, missing earnings and lost follow-up are excluded. The model does not establish that a particular pairing causes stability. Its additive log-rate structure assumes an earnings-split association shared across schooling groups; repeating it in two profiles is not independent confirmation of a special matching benefit. Read the full methods and independent numerical checks in the download.

## Does making it past a certain anniversary lower future divorce incidence?

**Longer-surviving marriages have lower observed annual divorce incidence in this cohort, but we did not identify a sharp “safe after year X” threshold.** Observed rates decline from about 16.7 per 1,000 person-years during years 0–<5 to 9.0 during 15–<20, 5.3 during 25–<30 and 2.8 during 30–<40. These are annual events per exposed time, not the probability of eventually divorcing.

The analysis splits each interview interval at the actual duration boundaries, assigning its time to the appropriate bands and a divorce only to the final segment. All 69,185 person-years and 592 divorces are preserved. The sample begins in midlife, so short marriages here often began later in life; this is **not a newlywed life table for couples marrying in their 20 s**.

The adjusted estimates below use one common ages 55–64 target. That makes every duration category possible; a 40-year marriage cannot be assigned to a 27-year-old. These values consequently describe an older comparison population and cannot serve as your current personal prediction.

blocks.title: Annual divorces per 1,000 married person-years: duration and uncertainty

blocks.text:
### A declining pattern is different from a proven cliff

The joint test for duration across all bands finds evidence of an overall association (7 degrees of freedom, p ≈ 0.023). **None of the seven adjacent-band comparisons establishes a clear step**, even before multiple-comparison adjustment; the smallest unadjusted p ≈ 0.135 and smallest Holm-adjusted p ≈ 0.945. This does not prove a smooth decline or rule out a real threshold; it means these data cannot locate one precisely. The 40+ band has only two divorces and particularly wide uncertainty.

“If still married after 20 years, what happens next?” is a **conditional** question about survivors. Some less-stable marriages have already ended, and spouses have also aged. The lower rate therefore does not show that merely waiting causes a troubled relationship to become safe. The common-age adjustment target contains only 60 observed divorces across 3,292 people, with sparse individual bands, so adjusted estimates borrow information through the model. No anniversary guarantees stability, and multiplying an annual rate by 5 or 10 does not produce a valid future 5-/10-year risk.

## Life events: what about years after the first child?

A new baseline-history extract checks subsequent annual divorce after the respondent’s first biological birth **within a first marriage**. The observed rate is about 8.8 per 1,000 person-years at 5–12 years since birth, 7.5 at 13–17, 5.8 at 18–24 and 3.3 at 25+. But respondents in the 5–12 group average age 42 and 14 married years; those in the 25+group average age 55 and 33 married years. These crude comparisons do not isolate a childbirth-stage association from age and marriage survival.

**This does not identify a birthday after which risk falls independently, or show that having a child prevents divorce.** The 0–4 year group contains only eight observed divorces. The explicitly no-first-birth group is shown for coverage, not as a randomized comparison with parenthood.

The measure is the respondent’s first biological child, not necessarily the current couple’s first shared child. Turning 18 does not establish that the last child moved out, so this is **not an empty-nest analysis**. A proper “event plus Y years” model needs the event date, same-couple linkage, a common follow-up horizon, and control of changing age and marriage duration. Job loss, illness, retirement and reconciliation need their own measured histories; this report does not infer them from zero wages or anniversaries.

blocks.title: First-birth stage at baseline: subsequent observed divorce incidence

blocks.text:
## Given your profile, which partner has the lowest statistical risk?

That is a useful target, but it needs evidence that **a partner characteristic works differently depending on your own characteristics**. A model that simply adds both spouses’ schooling and income does not establish a compatibility rule. We tested broad schooling-pair and own-schooling-by-earnings-role interactions rather than treating the earlier profile table as a personal matchmaking engine.

Neither interaction model improved prediction on people held out from fitting. Both-high-schooling interaction tests were uncertain (p ≈ 0.19 and 0.32); the joint own-schooling×earnings-role test hadp ≈ 0.11. Only 21 of 160 detailed sex×own-schooling×partner-schooling×total-wage×earnings-role cells met the exploratory 100-person/10-divorce support screen. This leaves too little reliable information to select an individualized minimum. Lack of improvement is not proof that compatibility never matters.

**What is supported:** broad schooling and earnings-configuration associations in the specified populations, with substantial uncertainty. **What is not yet supported:** a precise ideal partner’s degree, salary, denomination, age gap or political identity conditional on one person’s full profile. Detailed preference/relationship-quality variables and a younger marriage-start cohort would improve this question more than adding a spurious decimal place to the current estimates.

blocks.title: Held-out prediction improvement versus additive model: positive is better

blocks.text:
### Assets, work and schooling are separate inputs

A person can have no wage income while operating a business, holding substantial assets or receiving investment income. **Zero wages are not synonymous with unemployment or lack of resources.** The couple-profile model uses positive combined wage/salary earnings; wealth, portfolio income and self-employment profits are not interchangeable with that measure. Its older marriage sample also cannot be plugged directly into a forecast for a person in their 20 s.

For partner-search comparisons, separate your own age, education, earned income, business income and assets; then vary the prospective partner’s measured characteristics while keeping yours fixed. Changing an earnings share at fixed combined wages changes both spouses’ wage amounts, so the current share contrasts cannot by themselves answer “with my own income fixed, what partner income is best?” Nor do schooling-year tiers distinguish a master’s from a PhD. These are gaps for further analysis, not evidence that a particular partner type is safe.

## Annual comparisons and lower-divorce profiles

**Annual outcomes are the better starting point for this question, provided we compare people actually exposed to marriage during that period.** The earlier ACS denominator included every ever-married person, including people divorced long before the year. This extension uses a closer approximate at-risk denominator and fits the factors jointly, rather than interpreting each separately.

For comparable first marriages, **employment and education are substantial measured associations for both sexes; higher personal income is more consistently associated with lower annual divorce for men.** No degree or salary combination is proven to cause stability. A prospective NLSY person-time check is also included below, so current characteristics measured after divorce do not supply the only evidence.

### What changed to make the comparison fairer

The main profile analysis restricts ACS 2023 to adults 30–64 with only one marriage to date, no marriage in the preceding 12 months, and at least one calendar year since marriage. The approximate risk set includes those currently married or separated plus those reporting a divorce in the past 12 months. This removes many people with no marriage exposure during that year and excludes newlywed partial-year exposure.

The joint model includes **education, personal income, current employment, age at marriage, marriage duration and broad race/ethnicity controls**, separately for men and women. Profile predictions preserve the target population’s joint age-at-marriage/duration distribution; race is averaged as context, not used to define a desirable partner. All 80 replicate weights are used.

This is still an approximation: some widowhood exposure is omitted; reported marriage dates lack months; same-year divorce/remarriage is excluded by the one-marriage restriction; and income/employment may have changed after divorce. The fuller all-marriage model and old ever-married denominator remain in the downloadable sensitivity results.

### Which measured differences are largest?

In these predeclared comparisons, **unemployment has the largest point-estimate difference**: +0.63 percentage points for men and +1.09 for women versus employment. High school versus bachelor’s is +0.44 points for men and +0.61 for women. Income $200k+ versus $50k–74k is −0.46 points for men and −0.29 for women; the women’s income interval includes zero.

These differences use the same annual percentage-point scale within each model. They are adjusted associations, not estimated effects of interventions, and their intervals overlap—so the exact ordering is uncertain. The chosen contrasts matter: comparing unemployment with employment is a different change from adding a graduate degree. Marriage duration also strongly differentiates observed annual outcomes, but surviving 20 years is not an intervention, and survivor selection prevents calling it a protective treatment.

blocks.text:
### Practical profiles supported by the current data

**For a man:** college education, employment and stronger personal income describe a supported lower-divorce profile. In the first-marriage model, an employed bachelor’s profile with $100k–149k personal income is 0.84% (95% CI 0.74–0.95); at $200k+ it is 0.75% (0.63–0.87). A master’s does not improve on a bachelor’s consistently in this model.

**For a woman:** college education and avoiding unemployment have clearer support than simply maximizing personal salary. Among employed profiles, a master’s with $100k–149k is 1.26% (1.07–1.46); with $200k+ it is 1.12% (0.87–1.36). Corresponding bachelor’s profiles are 1.47% and 1.30%. The additional master’s association is modest and observational; professional/doctoral degrees do not establish a reliably better profile.

These are population-standardized annual divorce-report percentages for selected observed marriages, not your future spouse’s risk. They average across ages and durations rather than fixing an allegedly ideal wedding age. Neither table establishes that two separately modeled low-rate individuals will form a low-rate couple. A recommendation about matching spouses requires paired prospective histories.

blocks.text:
### Why the lowest modeled number is not an ideal partner prescription

The zero/negative-personal-income, not-in-labor-force bachelor’s profile for women produces about 0.31% (95% CI 0.26–0.36). It contains 15,222 respondents but only 23 reported divorces. The model can describe that association, but it cannot show that leaving work or giving up income would reduce divorce. Specialization within marriage, partner resources, selection into work, and post-divorce income changes can produce this pattern. Once income is controlled jointly, the broad female nonemployment contrast itself is small and inconclusive.

Likewise, optimizing every degree, age, income and employment cell would select noisy minima and poorly supported combinations. I used specified, observed profiles and retained their counts and uncertainty instead. This analysis does not measure fidelity, conflict skills, shared plans, relationship quality or a partner’s willingness to work on a marriage.

### Prospective annual follow-up changes what we can call protective

I constructed a second annual analysis from NLSY79:45,977 legally-married-or-separated interview intervals, 6,238 people, 1,463 observed divorces and about 91,579 unweighted person-years during 2000–2022. Exact reported interview/event months determine exposure; time ends at divorce, widowhood or follow-up. Predictors are measured before the interval. This is an event rate per person-year, unlike the ACS annual report proportion.

**Being already separated is by far the strongest immediate risk marker observed:** approximately 119 divorces per 1,000 person-years, compared with 8–10 among people reporting married at interval start. Adjusted rate ratios are 11.5 for men and 15.1 for women. This largely identifies marriages already on a dissolution pathway; it is not a partner-selection trait or evidence that preventing legal separation would fix the underlying marriage.

For education, work, income and attendance, the model without separation-state adjustment gives the comparisons below. Low family income predicts higher later divorce, particularly for women; some education/work associations remain uncertain. In this older cohort, graduate-educated women had a higher adjusted rate than high-school-educated women (RR 1.83, approximate 95% CI 1.22–2.74), despite the opposite credential pattern in recent ACS. This does not identify a harmful effect of graduate education; it shows that a universal ideal credential is unsupported across cohorts, populations and models. Adding baseline separation attenuates income associations and changes education estimates because it conditions on an important pathway/marker. These models should not be collapsed into a universal trait ranking.

blocks.text:
### Religion does not earn a place in an annual “ideal profile” from this analysis

The earlier NSFG association used current attendance and cumulative first-marriage histories. In prospective NLSY models, weekly attendance measured before later divorces does **not show a clear independent protective association** once other predictors are included. The same remains true when attendance is refreshed in 2012. Wide intervals permit meaningful increases or decreases; this is not proof that religious practice has no effect.

Therefore I would not require weekly attendance—or any specific denomination—in a statistically justified lower-divorce profile from these results. The paired prospective analyses below extend this check to both spouses’ earnings, schooling tiers and baseline religion. They do not establish a universal matching advantage. Exact graduate-degree pairings remain unavailable in that annual analysis; the earlier NSFG pairing finding remains historical.

The most defensible profile is **an intact relationship, college education where supported, employment/financial stability, and adequate combined resources**. Men’s personal income has a clearer recent ACS gradient; women’s own salary is less informative than a simple higher-is-always-better rule suggests. This is a supported descriptive sketch, not a proven ideal or a forecast for a new marriage.

## Pairing and demographic follow-up: what these comparisons actually establish

**Education level and educational matching are different questions.** Both-low and both-high couples match, yet their observed outcomes differ substantially. The new analysis separates levels, directions of mismatch, and explicit comparisons with balanced educational margins.

**Shared religion and more frequent attendance are not established guarantees.** A prospective couple-religion analysis is now available, but its approximately 100 events and broad intervals cannot identify an ideal denomination or frequency. Separate current-attendance associations in NSFG should not be read as prospective effects.

**Population overrepresentation depends on the denominator.** General-population divorce-event comparisons mix marriage exposure with divorce occurrence. Results below therefore show both all-adult and approximate marriage-exposed populations, with common age/sex standards. Demographic group averages do not establish an ideal partner ethnicity, individual compatibility, or the effect of changing an identity.

## Paired earnings: separate total resources from who earns more

A prospective NLSY79 analysis now links each baseline spouse’s prior-calendar-year wages to later legal-divorce incidence. It uses the same dollar thresholds for husbands and wives within a wave. The prespecified table below holds the husband in the upper positive-wage quartile; it does not search all configurations for the smallest outcome.

Adjusted relative-wage models additionally control combined couple-wage quartile, both spouses’ schooling tiers, respondent hours, age, current-marriage duration and wave. Versus balanced 40%–60% wife wages, husband-majority/both-positiveRR 0.72 (0.57–0.92), husband-onlyRR 0.96 (0.70–1.32), wife-majority/both-positiveRR 1.40 (1.01–1.94), wife-onlyRR 1.06 (0.70–1.61). This does not establish that a wife with zero wages is safer than two earners or financial dependence protects marriage. Baseline wage changes can already reflect marital problems; unmeasured conditions and missingness remain. Full schooling-pair matrices and model sensitivity are in the bundle; schooling years are not verified BA/master’s/doctorate credentials.

### Direct test of the high-husband/zero-wife-wages idea

Holding the husband in the same upper wage quartile, wife-zero incidence is 6.56 per 1000 person-years (4.56–9.44), versus 6.25 (3.79–10.30) when the wife is also in the upper quartile. Their formal crude rate ratio is 1.05 (0.56–1.95): the data do not identify wife-zero as better. All five wife wage bands are shown rather than selecting the minimum. “No reported wage/salary income” is not the same as no income, no wealth, or financial dependence.

blocks.text:
### Matching education does not explain away education level

After a shared age standard, first-marriage dissolution prevalence was 14.36% when both were BA+, 41.52% when both were below BA, and 32%–33% for either mismatch direction. Among wives below BA, a BA+ husband was associated with a lower point estimate than a below-BA husband; among BA+ wives, the below-BA husband group had the higher point estimate. A universal “matching is safer” interpretation does not describe this pattern.

blocks.title: First marriage dissolved by interview: age-standardized historical prevalence

blocks.text:
The broad BA-threshold mismatch directions differ by 1.09 percentage points (95% CI−8.00 to 10.18). An equal-cell comparison that balances each spouse’s marginal education distribution estimates mismatch-minus-match at 4.68 points (−2.07 to 11.43); with below-BA/bachelor/graduate-professional categories it is 0.70 points (−4.50 to 5.90). These estimates do not resolve a generic mismatch disadvantage beyond educational composition; they do not prove equivalence.

Exploratory logistic results depend on imposed additive partner-education assumptions. The 2 x 2 mismatch odds ratio is 1.40 (0.97–2.00); a 3 x 3 wife-higher term is 2.19 (1.12–4.30), while husband-higher is 0.65 (0.35–1.21). Those category/model-sensitive interaction terms should not override the direct cell comparisons or be described as independently causal mismatch effects. All detailed cells/models remain in the bundle.

blocks.text:
### Predissolution religion gives a more cautious answer

NLSY79 asks both respondent and spouse religion/attendance in 2000, before the 2000–2002 outcome interval. Different coded affiliations had 12.51 legal divorces per 1000 person-years (approximate 95% CI 8.05–19.44), compared with 11.88 (9.17–15.38) for the same coded affiliation. The adjusted mismatch rate ratio is 0.99 (0.59–1.66), controlling both spouses’ broad affiliation levels and age/sex/first-marriage age. This wide interval permits meaningful differences in either direction.

The named-Protestant mismatch group had 85 respondents and zero events. That supplies insufficient event information, not evidence of protection. Broad “Protestant/Christian/unspecified” and “other” codes are heterogeneous, so a code match is not proof of identical beliefs. The table includes both-none and exactly-one-none groups rather than assuming either is optimal.

All frequency levels are shown; choosing the smallest point estimate would manufacture an optimum from imprecise comparisons. Directional husband/wife weekly-pair cells are also too sparse for a strong husband-versus-wife rule; the only-wife-weekly cell has just 6 events.

## Population composition and annual divorce events

The new ACS analysis includes 1,499,259 respondents ages 30–64 and 13,788 past-year divorce reports. The approximate marriage-exposed denominator contains 978,402 respondents: currently married or separated, plus anyone reporting a past-year divorce. It reconstructs neither exact January 1 risk sets nor person-years. Overall annual event percentages are 1.01% per alladult and 1.59% per approximate exposed adult.

The first percentage in each table uses the entire general population, including never-married adults. The second uses the approximate marriage-exposed population. Both are standardized to a common age/sex distribution within their respective denominator. Groups can change relative position because marriage prevalence/exposure differs. These dated 2023 group associations do not establish inherent causes or select an ideal ethnicity or origin for an individual relationship.

blocks.text: Hispanic origin is an ethnicity; Hispanic respondents of every race form one category, and other rows are non-Hispanic (NH). The broad classifications combine varied people and histories. Age/sex adjustment does not remove differences in education, income, age at marriage, marriage duration, migration, or selection into marriage. Small NativeHawaiian/PacificIslander and some-other-race event cells are flagged; their point estimates should not be ranked as stable group characteristics.

### “Overrepresented” needs a reference population

A composition ratio above 1 means a group contributes a larger share of reported divorce events than of the selected marriage-exposed population; below 1 means a smaller share. The table states both shares. This is a crude composition calculation, not a new independent finding: algebraically it equals the group’s crude annual event proportion divided by the overall crude event proportion under the same denominator. Separate general-population representations are included in the CSV, and the preceding tables provide age/sex adjustment.

blocks.title: Crude event representation, with explicit marriage-exposed denominator

blocks.text:
### Birthplace, former nationality and family abroad remain different variables

“Native” includes U.S.-territory births and people born abroad to U.S.-citizen parents; it is not synonymous with birth in a U.S.state. Foreign-born origin rows use Census’s predefined world areas, not selected country rankings. Approximate years since entry are 2023 minus reported entry year, not lawful status, continuous residence or immigration timing relative to marriage.

Birthplace does not identify former nationality. ACS’s parent-nativity variable is restricted to eligible children age 17 orunder, so it cannot identify second-generation adults in this 30–64 analysis. Co-resident household relationships cannot establish whether parents, siblings or extended family live elsewhere in the U.S.or abroad. These requested dimensions cannot be inferred from the available adult microdata.20 partition checks across all 81 weights confirm the demographic totals, including foreign-born subgroup totals.

The prospective schooling analysis also does not resolve a residual mismatch association once both schooling levels and observed resources are controlled: husband-higherRR 1.08 (0.73–1.60), wife-higherRR 1.36 (0.90–2.06), versus the same schooling tier. These are schooling-year categories, not separately verified bachelor’s/master’s/doctorate degrees. The mismatch coefficient relies on additive partner-level assumptions; detailed matrices are retained.

### Age at first marriage: a bounded descriptive check

The first-marriage-only ACS model supplies the requested annual comparison below. These conditional predictive margins are affected by current-age 30–64 selection and survival of a first marriage into that sample. Forcing marriage-age categories across fixed observed current ages and durations can create infeasible combinations, so the smallest fitted value is not an optimal wedding age or a prospective recommendation. Age and marriage year have calendar-year resolution.

blocks.text:
## Political party: an annual check, with limited precision

Party affiliation was measured in 2008, before the 2008–2010 divorce interval. The primary model adjusts for age, sex, age at first marriage and baseline separation. Republican versus Democrat has an adjusted rate ratio of **0.88 (approximate 95% CI 0.51–1.51)**; Independent versus Democrat is **1.08 (0.65–1.80)**. These estimates do not resolve a clear difference.

Adding education, family income, race and earlier religious attendance changes the Republican estimate to 0.53 (0.29–0.97), but reduces the model from 4,069 people / 136 events to 3,366 / 112. On that same smaller sample, the simpler model is 0.69 (0.37–1.31). The result therefore depends on both sample and adjustment; selecting only the apparently significant specification would overstate the evidence. Only 20 Republican events support the extended estimate.

The table gives crude annual event rates, rather than the adjusted rate ratios above. These data cannot establish whether political agreement between spouses, ideological intensity or a specific policy view changes divorce risk. Religion is not a substitute for a measured political view.

blocks.text:
## Which additional datasets would help most?

**SIPP is the strongest next candidate for paired earnings and immigrant generation.** Census documents monthly marital status, month-specific spouse pointers, income and employment, plus biological parents’ nativity in the 2014 panel. That could support divorce exposure by month, lagged earnings for both spouses, and first/second-generation comparisons. Public-use availability and coding must be verified for the selected release, and a spouse must remain linked to the correct marriage after separation. [Official SIPP content](https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/sipp/about/sipp-content-information.html).

**NLSY 97 would test whether the NLSY79 findings carry to a younger cohort.** Its marriage and cohabitation event histories can link partners to characteristics including religion; the income module includes spouse/partner earnings. This is especially useful for the age-at-marriage question and education/religion pairing before dissolution. Exact wave coverage and event counts need a fresh audit. [Relationship histories](https://nlsinfo.org/content/cohorts/nlsy97/topical-guide/marriage-and-children/marital-marriage-relationships), [income documentation](https://www.nlsinfo.org/content/cohorts/nlsy97/topical-guide/income/income).

**PSID would add longer financial histories, wealth and family links.** Its public files include a marriage-history file and income/religion documentation. It is a strong candidate for distinguishing persistent earnings, job loss and accumulated resources. Public access requires registration and agreement to the provider’s terms; no registration or restricted-data access was completed here. [Getting started](https://psidonline.isr.umich.edu/GettingStarted.aspx), [documentation](https://psidonline.isr.umich.edu/Guide/documents.aspx).

**NSFH would add relationship quality, family obligations and gender-role attitudes.** Those variables address compatibility more directly than credentials alone, and the survey includes spouse/partner information and marital histories. Its much older fieldwork limits claims about contemporary marriages. [Survey archive](https://www.ssc.wisc.edu/nsfh/), [documented content](https://www.ssc.wisc.edu/nsfh/content2.htm).

**GSS panel files could extend politics and specific attitudes.** NORC provides panel datasets and a 2006–2014 panel codebook. A useful analysis would measure views before a later marital transition and audit usable divorce events; ordinary cross-sectional marital-status comparisons would not supply annual divorce risk. [Official downloads](https://gss.norc.org/get-the-data/stata.html), [documentation](https://gss.norc.org/get-documentation.html).

These are verified candidates for further work, not additional datasets already analyzed in this report. Priority: SIPP for monthly paired earnings and parental nativity, then NLSY 97 for cohort replication, then PSID for long-run finances. No single source has yet been verified to cover both spouses’ politics, detailed religion, earnings and relatives living abroad with enough divorce events.

## Supporting results from the earlier three-dataset analysis

The following sections retain the original annual, current-status and cumulative-history analyses. They answer different questions and should not be pooled into the annual profile estimates above.

## Executive Summary

- **Education is associated with divorce, but “more graduate education” does not yield a universal ranking.** In ACS 2023, age-standardized past-year divorce reports were 1.02% for bachelor’s-educated men and 1.16% for bachelor’s-educated women. All six master’s/professional/doctorate comparisons against bachelor’s within sex had 95% difference intervals containing zero; this does not establish equivalence.
- **Higher personal income is associated with lower annual divorce odds more clearly for men.** After controlling for age, education and race/ethnicity, men reporting $200k+ had an odds ratio of 0.66 (95% CI 0.57–0.76) versus $50k–74,999. Women’s estimate was 0.88 (0.73–1.07). Income and divorce were measured over overlapping periods, so these do not identify a pay effect.
- **Religious practice and spouse pairing add information.** NSFG first-marriage dissolution prevalence was about 26%–28% among weekly attenders versus 41%–42% among never attenders after interview-age standardization. Among women reporting both spouses BA+, unadjusted first-marriage dissolution prevalence was 14.5% (11.0–18.9), compared with 40.9% (36.1–45.8) when both were below BA. These are observed histories, not lifetime predictions; education and attendance may have changed after a dissolution.
- **NLSY79 supplies longer follow-up, with less precise small-degree estimates.** Recorded ever-divorce through the 2022/23 interview was 34.8% for bachelor’s-educated men and 40.0% for bachelor’s-educated women. These cohort estimates differ from both ACS annual measures and NSFG first-marriage histories. NLSY intervals here are weight-only approximations, not full survey-design intervals.

## Three different questions, three different denominators

**Cumulative recorded divorce occurrence — NLSY79:** among ever-married retained respondents born in 1957–1964, the fraction with at least one recorded legal divorce through their latest 2022/23 interview. This follows histories over decades, but is not complete lifetime risk or a common age/duration endpoint.

**Historical first-marriage dissolution prevalence — NSFG:** among ever-married people ages 25–49 interviewed in 2017–2019, the fraction whose first marriage had ended in divorce/annulment or separation by interview. Remarried people still count. Widowhood is excluded from the numerator but retained in the denominator. Follow-up exposure differs across people. A stricter divorce/annulment-only outcome is supplied separately.

**Annual divorce reporting — ACS:** among ever-married adults ages 30–64 interviewed in 2023, the fraction reporting divorce in the rolling past 12 months. This is not a calendar-year event rate, a person-year hazard, or the next-year risk of an intact marriage. The denominator includes previously divorced and widowed people.

**Current divorced prevalence — ACS:** the fraction currently divorced among ever-married adults. Remarriage removes people from this numerator; it does not erase a prior divorce. Current status therefore cannot substitute for ever-divorced history.

Do not add, average, or multiply these percentages into a personalized forecast. Sex refers to the survey’s male/female variable; the male and female samples are not matched spouses.

## Graduate degrees do not show a consistent annual-divorce hierarchy

The ACS analysis includes 1,499,259 respondents ages 30–64, of whom 1,182,597 were ever married; 13,788 ever-married respondents reported divorce in the past 12 months. Results use person weights and all 80 replicate weights, not a simple-random-sample approximation. Lower-education groups are not strictly monotonic either.

Matched-replicate differences against bachelor’s were small relative to uncertainty: for men, master’s −0.048 percentage points (95% CI −0.182 to 0.085); for women, master’s −0.090 points (−0.206 to 0.026). Professional and doctoral differences also included zero. These are pointwise exploratory intervals; “no detected difference” is not proof of equal outcomes.

### Current marital status answers a narrower question

The next table measures being divorced now, rather than experiencing a divorce during a year or ever. A person with a past divorce who remarried contributes to the denominator but not the current-divorced numerator.

blocks.title: Currently divorced among ever-married adults: age standardized

blocks.text:
## Higher pay is not a universal explanation

The income models adjust for five-year age groups, eight degree categories, and four race/ethnicity categories, separately for men and women. The reference group is **$50,000–74,999 in total personal income**, not household income or salary alone. Amounts use the ACS adjustment factor to express 2023 dollars.

For men, the $200k+ estimate is 0.66 (95% CI 0.57–0.76): about 34% lower odds of reporting a past-year divorce, conditional on these controls. For women, the estimate is 0.88 (0.73–1.07), which includes no association. No formal sex-interaction test was used, so differing significance alone does not prove the two associations differ.

Zero/negative-income women have an especially low adjusted odds ratio of 0.32. This is a warning against treating earnings as a simple protective dose: marital specialization, selection into employment, household resources, and income changes following divorce can all contribute. The model cannot distinguish these mechanisms.

blocks.title: Adjusted odds ratios: personal income versus $50k–74,999

blocks.text:
### Employment associations also differ across the samples

The employment model uses the same demographic controls, with employment replacing income. The reference is employed adults. Men outside the labor force have an adjusted odds ratio of 1.34 (1.23–1.46), while women outside the labor force have 0.57 (0.53–0.61). These describe employment near interview, not stable work across a marriage. The unstable small armed-forces subgroup is retained in downloadable results but omitted here.

blocks.title: Adjusted odds ratios: employment versus employed

blocks.text:
## NLSY79 provides decades of history, not a contemporary lifetime forecast

Among 5,562 ever-married respondents retained in 2022, recorded ever-divorce was 46.7% for men and 52.8% for women. The birth cohort is 1957–1964, ages 58–65 in nominal 2022 (some interviews occurred in 2023). Any recorded legal divorce counts, including divorce followed by remarriage. Combining marital status with transition records and baseline divorce dates identified 149 cases that all observed marital-status waves alone would miss.

Bachelor’s-educated men had 34.8% recorded ever-divorce and master’s-educated men 21.8%; women had 40.0% and 51.0%, respectively. The difference in direction from younger NSFG first-marriage histories is not a replication failure: the cohorts, exposure windows, any-marriage versus first-marriage outcomes, and final educational classifications differ. Degrees acquired after divorce are included. These results should not be read as the effect of obtaining a master’s.

**The following 95% intervals are weight-only approximations.** They account for unequal weights but omit survey clustering/stratification because usable design identifiers were not established for this extract. They can be too narrow. Among 2,681 respondents without a recorded divorce, 893 missed at least one marital-status wave. A complete-wave sensitivity retained the women’s master’s/bachelor’s difference (48.3% versus 37.3%), but does not eliminate selection bias. The doctoral groups contain only 21 men and 15 women; the professional groups contain 52 men and 29 women. Treat these as descriptive, fragile estimates.

blocks.title: Recorded ever-divorce through 2022/23: weight-only approximate 95% CIs

blocks.text:
### An earlier-income check supports a narrower association

A supplemental NLSY analysis starts with 3,502 people married in 2000 and retained in 2022, then looks for any recorded divorce in 2002–2022. Income was measured for 1999, before that outcome interval. Among men, subsequent recorded divorce was 29.9% below $25k versus 14.9% at $100k+, but the middle categories were not monotonic. Women’s corresponding estimates were 21.2% and 19.3%.

This improves temporal ordering but is unadjusted, selected on later retention, and uses **family income in nominal 1999 dollars**. It cannot answer whether moving someone’s current salary from $75k to $200k would change their divorce risk. The separate hours-worked results are also supplied: men working 2,000+ hours had 21.6% follow-up occurrence versus 30.8% at zero hours; women 24.5% versus 22.4%. These are descriptive, not effects of steady employment.

blocks.title: 1999 family income and later recorded divorce (approximate 95% CIs)

blocks.text:
## Younger adults’ first-marriage histories show a different slice

NSFG includes 1,908 ever-married men and 2,609 ever-married women ages 25–49. Bachelor’s and master’s groups show lower first-marriage dissolution prevalence than high-school-only groups in these unadjusted histories. Unlike the ACS annual measure, this counts a first marriage ending years earlier even if the respondent remarried. Unlike NLSY’s any-divorce outcome, later-marriage divorces after a first spouse’s death are not counted.

Doctorate/professional cells have only 23/31 men and 32/41 women. Wide intervals and different durations since marriage prevent a fine-grained graduate-degree ranking.

blocks.title: First marriage ended in divorce/annulment or separation by interview

blocks.text:
## Current religious practice is associated with marital history

After standardizing five-year interview-age groups within each sex, weekly-or-more attendance corresponds to 28.2% first-marriage dissolution prevalence among men and 26.4% among women; never attendance corresponds to 40.9% and 42.0%. The intermediate categories are not strictly ordered. Formal never-minus-weekly differences were 15.69 percentage points for women (95% CI 9.30–22.09) and 12.70 points for men (3.00–22.40), using the covariance of the survey influence estimates.

This is an association with **current attendance**, not religious commitment before marriage. Divorce can change participation or affiliation, and the survey cannot establish the causal direction here. Denomination tables and a divorce/annulment-only sensitivity outcome are included in the results; neither should be interpreted as a church-specific causal effect.

## Spouse education pairing can be examined without conditioning on marriage survival

Women’s NSFG first-husband education question is asked for former first husbands as well as current/separated husbands. The official questionnaire’s flow check C-12 on page 13 confirms this, although the codebook’s universe prose is incomplete. Observed responses cover all 2,722 ever-married women in the full file. Among eligible women ages 25–49, 21 with unknown/refused spouse education are excluded, leaving 2,588.

Both-BA+ pairings show 14.5% first-marriage dissolution prevalence, compared with 40.9% for both-below-BA pairings. Mixed pairings are around 33%–34%. After standardizing interview age, both BA+ was 14.36% (10.86–18.76) and both-below-BA 41.52% (36.66–46.54), a difference of −27.15 percentage points (−33.57 to −20.74). This age adjustment does not align marital duration or wedding-date covariates. This is more informative than analyzing only intact couples, but it is still a retrospective observational association. Spouses’ educational reports are not explicitly education at the wedding. Husbands’ graduate/professional education is combined; separate master’s/PhD/JD/MD pair-specific risks are unsupported. No corresponding former-first-wife education field was established for men.

ACS co-resident householder/spouse education tables are also supplied as descriptive distributions only. They exclude dissolved former couples and therefore cannot estimate divorce risk by pairing.

blocks.text:
## Correcting the starting benchmark

The earlier chat conflated several BLS quantities. Its 70.5% first-marriage-retention figure refers to **ever-married men with bachelor’s or higher** in a selected 1957–1964 cohort through age 55. It does not describe every college-educated man, both-college couples, high earners, or an effect of pay. “Not still in a first marriage” can include widowhood; the complement is not automatically divorce risk. The 27.1%/40.5% figures in that table describe first-marriage divorce, not ever-divorced-from-any-marriage prevalence.

The BLS study uses its own complete-history criteria and custom weights. This report’s NLSY analysis is a new, differently defined extract through 2022/23 rather than a replication of that published estimate. [BLS study and tables](https://www.bls.gov/mlr/2024/article/patterns-of-marriage-and-divorce-from-ages-15-to-55-evidence-from-the-nlsy79.htm).

## Methods, reproducibility and limits

**Data vintages.** ACS 2023 one-year national person files, NSFG 2017–2019 male/female respondent files, and NLSY79 public release through nominal 2022 were downloaded directly from Census/CDC/NLSinfo on October 19, 2026. These are intentionally specified releases, not a claim to use the newest available release. PSID was assessed but not analyzed: its download portal requires free registration, and no account was created.

**Uncertainty.** ACS uses successive-difference replication: variance=4/80×Σ (replicate estimate−full estimate)². All 80 replicate weights are retained; age standards and adjusted models are recalculated per replicate. Normal 95% intervals are used for proportions, with log-scale intervals for odds ratios. NSFG uses WGT 2017_2019, 18 strata and 72 nested PSUs; Taylor linearized variances use 54 design degrees of freedom and logit t intervals. NLSY uses positive 2022 weights and an independent-person weighted-ratio approximation; its intervals omit full survey design. No interval accounts for every source of recall, missingness, measurement error or model misspecification. Multiple comparisons are exploratory, with no multiplicity adjustment.

**Missingness and allocation.** ACS baseline retains Census-allocated responses; 8.13% of weighted ages 30–64 have the divorce-response allocation flag. Excluding these retains the broad degree pattern but shifts some values: women’s professional estimate changes from 1.17% to 1.26%. NSFG recoded family income is imputed; refused/unknown attendance and spouse education are excluded from the relevant domains, not coded never/low education. NLSY negative nonresponse/skip codes are excluded as specified; missed interviews may hide unrecorded divorces. Absence of a recorded transition is not proof of uninterrupted marriage.

**Confounding and selection.** Interview age standardization does not align marriage duration, age at marriage, marriage order or childhood conditions. Latest education, current religion, income and employment may follow divorce. Selection into marriage, remarriage, mortality, immigration, nonresponse and attrition affect the samples. These data do not justify multiplying “protective factors, ” claiming causation, or estimating a specific person’s probability. Wealth, fidelity/affairs, relationship quality and the exact effect of a salary increase are not answered by these analyses.

**Survival limits.** No headline lifetime or fixed-duration divorce risk is claimed. NSFG public duration dates are coarsened; an exploratory grouped four-year Kaplan–Meier calculation is retained in the machine-readable results, clearly labeled approximate, and excluded from conclusions. It depends on interval event/censoring conventions and treats death as censoring, not competing risk. A defensible wedding-baseline survival model with time-varying predictors would require further history harmonization.

**Validation.** Parsing counts were checked against NSFG codebooks, pair-question routing against the questionnaire, ACS totals and all replicate transformations were audited, and an independent optimizer reproduced the four ACS adjusted-model coefficient vectors to within 1.4×10⁻⁹. Graduate-degree difference CIs use matched replicate contrasts rather than inference from overlapping marginal CIs. Source-specific audit and model-check files are included. These checks validate computation and definitions, not causal identification.

The reproducibility bundle includes compact analytical datasets, all used weights/design variables, selected official dictionaries, raw NSFG files, source/checksum manifests, executable scripts, unrounded CSV results, and a single rerun entry point. Full Census and NLSY archives remain downloadable from the recorded official URLs and are checksum-identified. The report app source and figures are saved separately.

**Prospective uncertainty.** Prospective NLSY models use baseline-wave weights and person-time exposure, with respondent-cluster robust intervals for repeated intervals; the one-interval religion and politics analyses use independent-respondent robust intervals. These remain approximate because original survey PSU/stratum design variance and attrition-weight corrections were not established. The 2022-weight statement above applies to the original cumulative-history analysis only.

**Two downloads.** The hosted download contains aggregate tables, methods and code. Compact individual-level extracts, raw NSFG files and the larger local reproducibility archive are retained locally; official original microdata links remain in Sources.

- [CDC NSFG 2017–2019 data and design documentation](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/nsfg_2017_2019_puf.htm), [codebooks](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/nsfg/nsfg_2017_2019_codebooks.htm), [female first-husband questionnaire](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/data/nsfg/NSFG-PUF2017-2019-FemC-CRQ-508.pdf).
- [NLSY79 public archive through 2022](https://nlsinfo.org/cohort-data/nlsy79_all_1979-2022.zip), [official data-access guidance](https://www.nlsinfo.org/content/access-data-investigator/accessing-data-cohorts).
- [PSID public-data access portal](https://simba.isr.umich.edu/data/data.aspx), assessed for feasibility but not analyzed.

All reported analytical estimates were calculated from respondent microdata. Published findings were used only for documentation and to correct the original benchmark.
